content: Dermacentor variabilis, commonly referred to as the American dog tick or wood tick, is a species of hard tick that serves as a vector for several human diseases. These include Rocky Mountain spotted fever, caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, and tularemia, caused by Francisella tularensis. The transmission of these diseases occurs when the tick feeds on the blood of its host, a process that can take several days before symptoms manifest in the host. The life cycle of Dermacentor variabilis consists of four distinct stages: egg, six-legged larva, eight-legged nymph, and adult. Ticks require blood meals at each stage of their life cycle to survive and progress to the next stage. Hosts for these blood meals can include mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians. During their life cycle, ticks often switch between different hosts. Humans are most commonly targeted during the nymph and adult stages. The life cycle of ticks is influenced by seasonal variations, with eggs hatching into larvae during the summer months. Larvae typically infect bird or rodent hosts and remain with them until the following spring, at which point they molt into nymphs. Nymphs often seek mammalian hosts, including humans, and remain with their host until the fall, when they transition into adults. Adult ticks prefer larger mammalian hosts over smaller rodents. The complete life cycle of a tick generally spans three years, although variations may occur depending on the species. Dermacentor variabilis is associated with the transmission of several pathogens and diseases. These include: Anaplasma phagocytophilum, the causative agent of human granulocytic ehrlichiosis (HGE), and Ehrlichia chaffeensis, which causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis (HME). Tick paralysis, which results from the secretion of a neurotoxin by the tick. This condition leads to rapidly progressive flaccid quadriparesis, resembling Guillain-Barré syndrome. Rickettsia rickettsii, the causative agent of Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Francisella tularensis, the causative agent of tularemia. Although Dermacentor variabilis may be exposed to Borrelia burgdorferi, the bacterium responsible for Lyme disease, these ticks are not competent vectors for transmitting this particular disease.
